paper.title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces
paper.abstract: Abstract Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224 × 224 224{\times}224 , JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Unified multimodal models aim to understand and generate both images and text within a single model. Most current systems, however, treat the two modalities asymmetrically. In the dominant design, a pretrained autoregressive language model generates text and drives a diffusion or flow matching head that generates images [ 1 , 2 ] ; other models quantize images and generate both modalities as discrete tokens [ 3 , 4 ] . Either way, the two modalities are generated by different processes or through a quantizer, and the joint distribution is factorized in a fixed order: an output that contains both an image and text is produced one modality after the other, and the first cannot be revised in light of the second. Vision is also usually added to a model that was first pretrained on language, although controlled studies of multimodal pretraining find that late integration makes models lean on language priors and that training the modalities jointly from the start works better [ 5 ] . This suggests a different design: a model that treats both modalities alike, generates them with one process, and learns them together from the start. Such a design needs two things: a space in which one process can generate both modalities, and a source of knowledge for a backbone trained without a language model. Frozen pretrained encoders provide both. Their spaces are continuous for images and text alike and carry visual and linguistic knowledge learned at scale, and recent studies show that they are good generative targets for vision [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and for language [ 9 ] , although they were never built for generation. In these spaces, one flow matching process generates both modalities with the same objective, the same features serve as targets and as context, and a model of the joint distribution also contains its conditionals. Give each modality its own noise level and the two levels span a square (Figure 2 ). Text-to-image generation, captioning, and question answering hold one modality clean and move along an edge. Joint generation cuts through the middle, where image and text take shape together. To build a working model on this idea, we had to settle four questions that existing unified models leave open: whether text should be generated as continuous states or kept as tokens, which denoising tasks to train on, which encoder spaces to read and write, and whether these answers still hold as the model grows. We introduce JUICE ( J oint U nified multimodal modeling I n C ontinuous E ncoder spaces; Figure 1 ), a unified model that works directly in the continuous spaces of frozen pretrained image and text encoders. A single flow matching backbone, MM-RiT, trained from scratch, connects the image and text streams through bidirectional joint attention [ 10 ] , and each stream has its own noise scale and schedule. We train MM-RiT on both the edges and the interior of the square, with conditional and joint denoising. At inference, a task is a path through the square: keeping some streams clean ( t = 1 t=1 ) and generating the others gives text-to-image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or coupled joint generation (Section 3 ). Figure 1: JUICE overview. (a) Continuous image and text representations from frozen encoders share one MM-RiT backbone via bidirectional joint attention. Appendix A.3 explains the details of each block. (b) Conditional tasks (text-to-image, visual question answering) and joint reasoning (maze solving) use the same interface by assigning clean context ( t = 1 t{=}1 ) and generation targets ( t < 1 t{<}1 ). Our pretraining studies (Section 4 ) change one design choice at a time and keep the rest of the recipe fixed. (i) Generative frameworks. At a shared guidance scale, JUICE scores 48.41 GenEval and a model trained only for text-to-image generation scores 47.86, while all three frameworks that write text as tokens fall below that model. Captions generated as continuous states lose some exact wording but match the images as well as autoregressive captions do. (ii) Training task mixtures. Training should cover the regions that sampling visits: joint and conditional denoising together outperform either one alone, beyond the effect of supervising more targets. (iii) Representation spaces. The VAE reconstructs better than the semantic encoders, yet generation and captioning both work better in the semantic spaces, and Flan-T5 states beat larger text embedding models. (iv) Scaling. From 179M to 2.1B backbone parameters, SigLIP2 [ 11 ] , which is aligned with language, writes better captions at every size, while the early lead of WebSSL-DINO [ 12 ] (DINO) in image generation disappears. With these answers in hand, we train two 2.1B models that pair Flan-T5 with SigLIP2 or with DINO (Section 5 ). Working at 224 × 224 224{\times}224 and starting from no language model, each uses one set of weights for compositional image generation, generation that needs world knowledge, and visual question answering. The two reach 0.87 and 0.88 GenEval, and the SigLIP2 model reaches 85.22 on DPG-Bench, 0.45 on WISE [ 13 ] , and 73.1 on VQAv2. Because JUICE models the joint distribution, it can also reason jointly across modalities: with coupled sampling, the image and its text are generated together, each conditioning on the other’s evolving state. We adapt JUICE to two planning tasks, mazes with multiple solutions [ 14 ] and visual spatial planning [ 15 ] , in which it draws a route on the map and writes the matching moves. Sampled independently, the two outputs often disagree on mazes: the model draws one valid route and writes out a different one, and joint success is only 54.6%. Generating one modality first repairs this, but the result then depends on the order (95.2% with the image first, 85.3% with the text first), and nothing says in advance which order to use. Coupled sampling reaches 93.7% without making that choice. In the two cases we trace, whichever output settles later rewrites itself to match the other. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at the training sizes, and 94% and 69% at two larger sizes it never saw in training. Our main contributions are: 1. Joint modeling in pretrained representation spaces. We propose JUICE, which models the joint distribution of images and text in the continuous spaces of frozen pretrained encoders with one flow matching Transformer trained from scratch. With a noise level for each modality, every task is a path through one square, with no fixed generation order. 2. Systematic design studies. Section 4 reports controlled pretraining runs on how text is generated, which tasks are trained, and which encoder spaces are used, plus a scaling study from 179M to 2.1B parameters. We summarize what they show as four takeaways for continuous joint modeling. 3. Scaling and joint reasoning. A single set of 2.1B weights handles compositional image generation, generation that needs world knowledge, and visual question answering (Section 5 ). On two planning tasks, coupled sampling gets the drawn route and the written moves to agree without a fixed generation order (Section 5.4 ).

sections.heading: Unified multimodal models.
sections.text: Most unified models are hybrids that combine different representation spaces and generative processes (Table 1 ). Chameleon [ 16 ] models discrete text tokens and quantized image codes autoregressively. Transfusion [ 17 ] pairs autoregressive text with diffusion over continuous image latents, and Show-o [ 20 ] pairs autoregressive text with diffusion over discrete image tokens. MMaDA [ 3 ] and Muddit [ 4 ] use discrete masked diffusion for both modalities, while D-DiT [ 18 ] combines discrete masked diffusion for text with continuous flow for images. D-DiT and Muddit start from pretrained image generators, Show-o and MMaDA from pretrained language models, and Chameleon and Transfusion are trained from scratch. In most of these models, the two modalities are generated by different processes, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order. JUICE instead generates both with one flow matching process in frozen representation spaces and is trained from scratch; Section 4.2 compares it with representative formulations under the same recipe.

sections.heading: Generation in pretrained representation spaces.
sections.text: Representation autoencoders (RAEs) [ 6 , 7 ] show that diffusion works well on frozen pretrained visual features, whose semantic structure makes them good targets. Beyond Language Modeling (BLM) [ 8 ] takes up this idea and trains a unified backbone from scratch with flow matching over frozen visual features, while language is still predicted autoregressively as discrete tokens. Other unified models pick different visual targets. Show-o2 [ 1 ] still generates VAE latents, which it processes semantically. TUNA [ 21 ] aligns unified features built from VAE latents, and Tuna-2 [ 2 ] removes the visual encoders altogether and generates pixels. For text, ELF [ 9 ] applies continuous flow matching directly in pretrained text representation spaces, though only to generate text on its own. Each of these works generates only one modality in a continuous representation space: BLM still predicts text as tokens, and ELF generates no images. JUICE generates both modalities in pretrained spaces with one process, so the same representations serve as generation targets and as cross-modal context, and Sections 4.4 and 4.5 study which spaces suit this joint use and how the answer changes with scale.

sections.heading: Joint and conditional multimodal modeling.
sections.text: Separate noise schedules for each modality [ 19 , 22 ] provide a mathematical framework for a single model to capture the marginal, conditional, and joint distributions of images and text. Existing implementations, however, need specialized components. UniDiffuser [ 19 ] diffuses CLIP embeddings and needs a separate autoregressive GPT-2 to decode text; OneFlow [ 23 ] models text with discrete edit flows. OmniFlow [ 24 ] uses rectified flow for generation from any modality to any other. Its MMDiT backbone starts from Stable Diffusion 3, and its text latent comes from a VAE built on Flan-T5 and TinyLlama. JUICE keeps both modalities as continuous encoder states with one state per token, decodes text with a lightweight parallel decoder, and trains one backbone on them from scratch. In this setting, joint denoising improves conditional generation by more than its extra targets explain (Section 4.3 ), and coupled sampling lets the two streams settle on the same one of several valid solutions (Section 5.4 ).

sections.heading: Continuous diffusion for language.
sections.text: Early work diffused learned word embeddings and rounded them back to tokens (Diffusion-LM [ 25 ] , DiffuSeq [ 26 ] ); later work improved the likelihood objectives (CDCD [ 27 ] , Plaid [ 28 ] ). Flow matching over categorical distributions, which places each token on the probability simplex, offers another continuous route to discrete data such as text [ 29 , 30 ] . A second line of work diffuses directly in the representation spaces of pretrained language models, either after compressing sequences into fixed latents (LD4LG [ 31 ] ) or over contextual encoder states (TEncDM [ 32 ] , ELF [ 9 ] ). JUICE follows the second line for its text stream and diffuses contextual encoder states. Unlike these text only models, it generates the states jointly with images, and Section 4.2 compares this choice with discrete text under one recipe.

sections.heading: 3  Method
sections.text: As shown in Figure 1 , JUICE operates directly in the continuous representation spaces of frozen pretrained encoders, using a single flow matching Transformer (MM-RiT) trained from scratch. The same model supports generation, understanding, and joint tasks over images and text simply by varying which representations are provided as clean inputs and which are generated from noise. Section 3.1 reviews flow matching, Section 3.2 presents the formulation, and Sections 3.3 to 3.5 describe the architecture, training procedure, and inference; Appendix A.6 provides implementation details.

sections.text: JUICE models the joint distribution of an image representation z i z_{\mathrm{i}} and a text representation z t z_{\mathrm{t}} , both extracted from frozen pretrained encoders (Section 3.3 ). Each modality has its own time t m ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t_{m}\in[0,1] , and a single network predicts both clean states from the pair of noisy states: ( z ^ i , z ^ t ) = f θ ​ ( z i t i , z t t t , t i , t t ) . (2) The pair of times lives in a unit square, the 2D time domain of Figure 2 . Setting t m = 1 t_{m}{=}1 makes modality m m a clean condition, and any t m < 1 t_{m}{<}1 means it is still being generated. A task is thus just a path through the square. Text-to-image generation follows the edge t t = 1 t_{\mathrm{t}}{=}1 and captioning the edge t i = 1 t_{\mathrm{i}}{=}1 , while joint generation cuts through the interior. Question answering sets times per token, so the image and the question stay at t = 1 t{=}1 while the answer is generated (Appendix A.6.2 ). We therefore train on the edges with conditional denoising and on the interior with joint denoising, so that every region sampling passes through is covered. The formulation introduces three requirements, each addressed by one design component. First, because the two representation spaces differ in dimensionality and feature statistics, each modality has its own projections, noise scale, and noise schedule (Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). Second, because any token can be either a condition or a generation target, time tokens in the sequence and a time embedding for each token tell the network the role of each position (Section 3.3 ). sections.heading: 3.3  Architecture
sections.text: Representation Encoders. Given a paired image x i x_{\mathrm{i}} and text x t x_{\mathrm{t}} , frozen pretrained encoders extract features that are normalized to align their scales with the diffusion noise [ 35 ] : h m = E m ​ ( x m ) , z m = N m ​ ( h m ) , m ∈ { i , t } . h_{m}=E_{m}(x_{m}),\qquad z_{m}=N_{m}(h_{m}),\qquad m\in\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{t}\}. (3) SigLIP2 [ 11 ] and Flan-T5-Small [ 36 ] are our default image and text encoders, and Section 4.4 looks at other choices. We do not finetune the encoders. Their spaces already encode visual and linguistic knowledge learned at scale, and if they stay fixed, the same features can be used both as targets to generate and as context to condition on. Multimodal Representation Diffusion Transformer (MM-RiT). MM-RiT implements f θ f_{\theta} in Equation 2 : it receives both streams at independently specified noise levels ( t i , t t ) (t_{\mathrm{i}},t_{\mathrm{t}}) [ 19 ] and predicts both denoised clean states, which we convert to velocities for training (velocity matching loss) and inference (ODE solver). To accommodate the distinct image and text representation spaces, each MM-RiT block uses separate Q/K/V projections for each modality, concatenates the resulting sequences for one bidirectional joint attention operation, and then applies separate output projections and feedforward networks [ 7 , 8 , 37 ] . Time tokens in the sequence and additive time embeddings for each token expose the noise level of each modality and each token, so the network can distinguish clean conditioning positions ( t = 1 t{=}1 ) from generation targets ( t < 1 t{<}1 ). Representation Decoders. Fixed decoders map the generated representations back to pixels and tokens at inference: x ^ i = D i ​ ( z i ) , x ^ t = D t ​ ( z t ) . \widehat{x}_{\mathrm{i}}=D_{\mathrm{i}}(z_{\mathrm{i}}),\qquad\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{t}}=D_{\mathrm{t}}(z_{\mathrm{t}}). (4) For images we use the Scale-RAE decoder that belongs to the image encoder [ 7 ] . For text, a lightweight parallel decoder maps all generated states to tokens in one forward pass, which is much faster than autoregressive decoding; the pretraining study and the final models each use one decoder of this design. All decoders are trained separately and stay fixed during MM-RiT training. Appendix A.4 describes them and compares parallel with autoregressive decoding.

sections.heading: 3.5  Inference
sections.text: Conditional and Joint Generation. At inference, conditioning inputs stay at t = 1 t{=}1 , and generation targets are integrated from Gaussian noise up to t = 1 t{=}1 . Text-to-image, image-to-text, and joint generation differ only in the path they take through the 2D time domain [ 19 ] (Figure 2 ): ( t i ​ ( s ) , t t ​ ( s ) ) = { ( S α i ​ ( s ) , 1 ) , T2I , ( 1 , S α t ​ ( s ) ) , I2T , ( S α i ​ ( s ) , S α t ​ ( s ) ) , joint , s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . (t_{\mathrm{i}}(s),\,t_{\mathrm{t}}(s))=\begin{cases}(S_{\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}}(s),\;1),&\text{T2I},\\[2.0pt] (1,\;S_{\alpha_{\mathrm{t}}}(s)),&\text{I2T},\\[2.0pt] (S_{\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}}(s),\;S_{\alpha_{\mathrm{t}}}(s)),&\text{joint},\end{cases}\quad s\in[0,1]. (6) Classifier-Free Guidance. For conditional tasks we apply classifier-free guidance [ 38 ] in velocity space: the prediction with the condition is pushed away from a reference prediction without it, which strengthens what the condition adds. No training stage drops the condition, so JUICE has no learned null token. The reference instead replaces the condition with an uninformative input that the model has learned to handle. For an image condition, the image is placed at its noise end, a state the joint task trains the model to see next to text; for a text condition, we use the clean states of the generic caption “a photo.”, which says almost nothing about the image. We use w = 5 w{=}5 for text-to-image generation, w = 3 w{=}3 for captioning and question answering, and no guidance for joint generation and planning. Appendix A.6.2 gives the formulas, and Table 20 compares the text reference with placing the caption at its noise end. Coupled Sampling. In joint generation, both velocity fields are computed from the current joint state ( z i t i , z t t t ) (z_{\mathrm{i}}^{t_{\mathrm{i}}},z_{\mathrm{t}}^{t_{\mathrm{t}}}) before either modality is updated. We call this coupled sampling . Each stream is thus conditioned, step by step, on the other stream as it evolves. Independent sampling works differently. It integrates each stream separately and leaves the other one at its initial noise for the whole trajectory, which amounts to sampling each modality from its marginal. Sequential sampling first generates one modality completely and then the other conditioned on it, with either the image or the text going first.

sections.heading: 4  Pretraining Study
sections.text: Putting both modalities in continuous encoder spaces under one denoiser raises the four questions of Section 1 , and this section takes them in turn. Should text be generated as continuous states or as tokens (Section 4.2 )? Which denoising tasks should training cover (Section 4.3 )? Which encoder spaces should the model read and write (Section 4.4 )? And do the answers change with model size (Section 4.5 )? All runs share the setup below, and each study ends with a takeaway.

sections.heading: 4.1  Setup
sections.text: All studies share one pretraining recipe and vary one design choice at a time. The reference model has an MM-RiT backbone with 668M trainable parameters over frozen SigLIP2-SO400M image features and Flan-T5-Small text states. It is trained for 50k updates at a global batch size of 4,096 with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}{=}0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}{=}0.95 , weight decay 0.01) and a constant learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4{\times}10^{-4} after 5,000 warmup steps, on 38M pairs of images and captions [ 39 , 7 ] and Cambrian-7M [ 40 ] , using the default task ratios (55.6% joint, 22.2% T2I, 22.2% I2T; Appendix A.6.1 ). For image generation we report GenEval (GE) [ 41 ] and DPG-Bench (DPG) [ 42 , 43 ] , with 25 Euler steps and guidance w = 5 w{=}5 against the generic caption reference (a fully masked caption for the base D-DiT-style framework; Appendix A.6.2 ). For captioning we report CIDEr [ 44 ] and CLIPScore (CLIP, × 100 \times 100 ) [ 45 ] on 5,000 pairs held out from training, with 16 steps and w = 3 w{=}3 (Section 3.5 ). Each configuration is trained once. The framework and representation comparisons change complete pipelines, since a representation comes with its own decoder, normalization, and noise settings; they therefore compare design choices as they would be deployed rather than isolated components. Appendices A and B give the full configurations.

sections.heading: 4.2  Generative Frameworks

sections.heading: Image generation.
sections.text: JUICE reaches 48.41 GenEval and 78.85 DPG, the highest of the four frameworks. Part of this lead comes from the condition encoder: the discrete text frameworks condition image generation on learned token embeddings, whereas JUICE conditions on contextual T5 states. With the same frozen T5 condition, all three improve (Transfusion-style goes from 44.23 to 46.07 GenEval), but none of them reaches JUICE. A model trained only for text-to-image generation gets 47.86 at the same guidance scale. Adding a continuous text stream thus leaves image generation intact at this scale (48.41), whereas every token text stream lowers GenEval, with or without the T5 condition (for MMaDA-style, the image process also changes). With the condition matched, what remains different is the text stream: JUICE trains both streams with the same flow matching objective, while the discrete text frameworks train them with different objectives and attention patterns. With the guidance scale tuned per model, the T2I only model peaks at w = 3 w{=}3 (51.23) and leads JUICE by 2.8 points (Appendix A.6.2 ). sections.heading: Captioning.
sections.text: On the alignment between captions and images, JUICE matches autoregressive text (80.20 vs. 80.37 CLIPScore). On n-gram agreement with the reference captions, it is the weakest of the four: its CIDEr (88.80) is just over half that of autoregressive text (160.52) and below D-DiT-style masked text diffusion (115.22). The gap lies mainly in the generated states, not in the parallel caption decoder of this study, which recovers 99.2% of tokens from clean T5 states (Table 29 ; Appendix A.4.2 ). The captions thus describe the image content as well as autoregressive ones but word it differently from the references. This is the pattern expected when errors in a generated continuous state move it toward nearby states with a similar meaning: the wording changes more than the content. Takeaway: Continuous text spares images but costs wording. Of the four frameworks, only the one with continuous text keeps up with a model trained only for text-to-image generation on GenEval at the shared guidance scale (48.41 vs. 47.86); the three token text frameworks all fall below it, even with the T5 condition. Continuous text pays in CIDEr instead (88.80 vs. 160.52 for autoregressive text), while its CLIPScore is on par.

sections.heading: 4.3  Training Task Mixtures
sections.text: Because both modalities are continuous and each has its own noise level, JUICE can be trained not only on conditional tasks, where one modality is clean, but also on joint denoising, where both are noisy and each is predicted next to a noisy partner. In the 2D time domain ( t i , t t ) (t_{\mathrm{i}},t_{\mathrm{t}}) , the conditional T2I and I2T tasks lie on the edges and joint denoising covers the interior (Section 3.4 ; Figure 2 ). We explore what joint denoising brings and which regions training should cover: Table 3 compares five recipes, and Figure 4 follows two of them, Mixing and Multi-task, over training. sections.heading: Edges and interior.
sections.text: Training in a single direction specializes: the T2I only and I2T only models do well in the direction they are trained for and fail in the other. Training only the edges (Multi-task) supports both directions, but training only the interior (Joint only) is worse on all four metrics. Joint only never sees the boundary. At conditional inference the condition is exactly clean, and training on the interior never produces that state. Mixing trains on both and is the best bidirectional recipe on every metric; it also stays ahead of Multi-task throughout training. The rule is simple: train where sampling goes. T2I and I2T sampling follow the edges, while joint sampling goes through the interior. At the shared guidance scale, Mixing is as good as the T2I only model at image generation, but it is still behind the I2T only model on CIDEr (88.80 vs. 107.22). The ordering of the bidirectional recipes also holds with the guidance scale tuned per recipe: with each recipe at its best scale in w ∈ [ 1 , 5 ] w\in[1,5] , Mixing (48.41) still leads Multi-task (44.29) and Joint only (31.33) on GenEval, while T2I only rises to 51.23 (Appendix A.6.2 ).

sections.heading: More targets or cross-modal exchange?
sections.text: Extra supervision explains only part of the gain. Mixing does supervise each modality more often than Multi-task (on 77.8% vs. 50% of examples), so we control for target count (lower block of Table 3 ; Appendix B.2.1 ). One control replaces each joint example with two conditional ones at the same target count (matched dual conditional, DC), at 1.56 times the backbone work; another blocks cross-modal attention on joint examples. Both lower every metric relative to Mixing, by 2.51 and 2.92 GenEval points, respectively. In the other direction, a joint branch that keeps both streams noisy but supervises only one of them (single target joint) beats Multi-task on all four metrics with the same number of targets. Training Multi-task for longer, until it sees as many targets as Mixing, closes the CIDEr gap (89.31) but not the GenEval gap (43.16). The noisy partner and the exchange with it each contribute. Takeaway: Train where you sample. Sampling uses both the edges of the square and its interior, and training has to cover both. Joint only never sees a clean condition and reaches just 31.33 GenEval at its best guidance scale; Multi-task never trains on the interior and reaches 44.29; Mixing gets 48.41. Matching the target count does not close the gap, so the joint examples give more than extra supervision.

sections.heading: 4.4  Representation Spaces
sections.text: JUICE reads and writes in the spaces of its frozen encoders, so the encoder determines both what the model sees and what it must generate. Encoders differ in what their spaces capture: some are trained to reconstruct their input, others to capture semantics, and some are aligned with the other modality. We explore these tradeoffs on both sides. With T5 fixed for text, we compare SigLIP2 [ 11 ] and WebSSL-DINO [ 12 ] (DINO) image features with FLUX VAE latents [ 46 ] and raw pixels [ 34 , 2 ] . With SigLIP2 fixed for images, we compare T5 with Qwen3-Embedding (Qwen3-E) [ 47 ] , Qwen3-VL-Embedding (Qwen3-VL-E) [ 48 ] , and SigLIP2 text features (Figure 5 ; full metrics in Table 28 ). Figure 5: Semantic encoder spaces outperform VAE latents and pixels, and T5 leads among text spaces. Top: image spaces with T5 text. Bottom: text spaces with SigLIP2 images.

sections.heading: Image spaces.
sections.text: Semantic encoders outperform spaces built for reconstruction on all four metrics: SigLIP2 and DINO reach 48.41 and 49.07 GenEval, against 35.42 for the VAE and 24.48 for pixels. This ordering is broadly the reverse of reconstruction quality, as the FLUX VAE reconstructs best among the learned spaces (ImageNet rFID 0.288, against 0.435 for SigLIP2; Table 30 ). The two semantic encoders are close on image generation, but captioning separates them: SigLIP2, which is aligned with language, leads DINO by 20.0 CIDEr and 8.5 CLIPScore. For a model that both generates and conditions on the same features, semantic structure thus matters more than reconstruction fidelity. The order of the two semantic encoders on image generation changes with model size (Section 4.5 ).

sections.heading: Text spaces.
sections.text: Flan-T5 states lead on all four metrics, ahead of larger embedding models and of SigLIP2 text features, which are aligned with the image space. Each text space is decoded with its own parallel decoder, which recovers 97.5% to 99.2% of tokens from clean states, and even a linear readout recovers 96.5% to 98.5% (Table 29 ). All four spaces thus retain most of the token information. The decoder affects only the captioning metrics, and the GenEval differences, which do not involve it, indicate that the ordering reflects how well each space serves as a generation target and condition. Qwen3-E comes close to T5 on CIDEr (88.50 vs. 88.80) but trails it by 5.3 GenEval points, and the SigLIP2 text features give the lowest GenEval (33.08). Alignment with the image space therefore does not make a text space a better target or condition here. Takeaway: Semantics over reconstruction. Good reconstruction does not make a good generation space. The FLUX VAE has the best rFID among the learned spaces (0.288 vs. 0.435 for SigLIP2), but GenEval in it drops to 35.42, from 48.41 with SigLIP2. SigLIP2 and DINO are close on generation, and SigLIP2’s alignment with language shows up in captioning (20.0 CIDEr ahead). On the text side, Flan-T5 states beat larger embedding models and SigLIP2 text features.

sections.heading: 4.5  Scaling
sections.text: Do these preferences survive as the model grows? Keeping the recipe above, we train MM-RiT backbones from 179M to 2.1B trainable parameters (d12 to d28; Appendix A.5 ) on both the SigLIP2 and the DINO image space (Figure 6 ). All four metrics improve with size in both spaces, but scale treats the two roles of the image space differently. For image generation the order flips. DINO is well ahead at 179M (32.90 vs. 18.99 GenEval), the gap shrinks as the backbone grows, and by 2.1B SigLIP2 is ahead (56.81 vs. 52.78). Captioning shows no such flip: SigLIP2 leads at every size and reaches 86.64 CLIPScore at 2.1B, against 72.32 for DINO. The two trends separate the roles of the image space: DINO’s advantage as a generation target at small scale fades as capacity grows, whereas the benefit of SigLIP2’s language alignment for producing text persists. After finetuning, the two 2.1B models of Section 5 differ by less than 0.02 GenEval (DINO 0.88, SigLIP2 0.87), so neither image space keeps a clear GenEval advantage, while SigLIP2 leads on almost every understanding benchmark. Figure 6: Scaling the backbone from 179M to 2.1B parameters. DINO’s early lead in image generation disappears with scale, while SigLIP2 leads captioning at every size. DPG-Bench in this figure uses the time swap text reference (Appendix A.6.2 ). Takeaway: Scale reorders image spaces for generation, not captioning. DINO’s lead in image generation fades as the model grows, while SigLIP2’s language alignment helps captioning at every size.

sections.heading: 5  Experiments
sections.text: A single model of the joint distribution of images and text should provide three abilities: generating images from text, answering questions about images, and producing image and text outputs that are individually correct and mutually consistent. We now evaluate JUICE on each of them at scale.

sections.heading: 5.1  Setup
sections.text: We train two 2.1B models, one per image space. Each is pretrained with the recipe of Section 4.1 , but for 60k instead of 50k updates, and then finetuned for 15k updates at a global batch size of 1,024 on 20.6M text-to-image and visual understanding examples (Appendix A.7 ). Text-to-image generation uses 25 Euler steps with guidance w = 5 w{=}5 ; visual question answering uses 16 steps with w = 3 w{=}3 , with the parallel decoder reading out all answer positions at once. For joint reasoning, we adapt the finetuned models to each task separately (both models to mazes, the SigLIP2 model to visual spatial planning), read the moves with a linear head trained for each task, and sample without guidance (Section 5.4 ). All input and output images are 224 × 224 224{\times}224 . We compare with unified models of 1B to 3B parameters; Appendix C includes comparisons with larger models.

sections.heading: Generation with world knowledge.
sections.text: WISE [ 13 ] checks whether generated images reflect the world knowledge a prompt implies, with cultural, temporal, spatial, biological, physical, and chemical categories (Table 5 ). At the guidance scale used for GenEval, the SigLIP2 variant has a WiScore of 0.45. This is the highest overall score among unified models of 1B to 3B parameters that report one (which reach at most 0.41) and above Janus-Pro-7B (0.35), though below FLUX.1-dev (0.50) and BAGEL (0.52); OneFlow reports only the cultural category, where it scores higher. WISE, unlike GenEval, separates the two image spaces: SigLIP2 scores 0.45 and DINO 0.37. The advantage that Section 4.4 found for SigLIP2 in captioning thus carries over to generation that needs world knowledge. The difference is largest for cultural prompts (0.41 vs. 0.31) and smallest for spatial ones (0.62 vs. 0.59), where the SigLIP2 variant is level with FLUX.1-dev. Its lead over Harmon, the strongest baseline of 1B to 3B parameters, comes mostly from spatial and physical prompts, and it is slightly lower on biology (0.35 vs. 0.37). Since JUICE has no language model backbone, this knowledge comes from its frozen encoders and its training data. A lower guidance scale with the time swap reference raises both scores, to 0.49 and 0.42, respectively (Appendix A.6.2 ). Figure 8 shows one example per category.

Figure 9 shows eight selected questions of seven types, from attributes and counting to chained spatial relations, outside knowledge, and object existence, which both variants answer correctly; both also produce fluent, concise captions (Appendix E.2 ). Longer outputs are less reliable. The detailed descriptions in Appendix E.4 get the main objects, colors, and layout right but contain grammatical errors and the occasional invented word, in line with the lexical cost seen in Section 4.2 . Reading out the answer states in parallel loses little: on VQA with open answers, an autoregressive decoder on the same states is within 1.5 points but 2.1 to 6.4 times slower on these short answers. It is much worse on most multiple choice benchmarks (45.3 vs. 66.0 on MMBench), but only the parallel decoder saw multiple choice answers in training (Appendix A.4.2 ).

sections.heading: 5.4  Joint Reasoning
sections.text: Some tasks need an image and a text output that are each correct and that agree, such as a route drawn on a map and the moves that describe it. When several answers are valid, being correct is not enough: the two outputs must also commit to the same answer. Sampling each modality from its own marginal can pick a different valid answer in each, which we call a cross-modal mode mismatch. A model of the joint distribution can instead produce both outputs together, with each modality conditioning on the other’s evolving state (coupled sampling; Section 3.5 ). We first look at unconditional joint generation and then turn to two planning tasks, in which the input is a map image and a text question and the model generates the map with the route drawn on it together with the move sequence.

sections.heading: Joint generation.
sections.text: Without any condition, both streams start from noise and the model generates an image and a caption together (selected samples in Figure 10 ). sections.text: Our grid mazes have two to sixteen shortest routes each [ 14 ] , so both outputs can be valid and still disagree. For each training pair, one of these routes is picked at random. At evaluation, any shortest route counts, and a joint success (J) needs both outputs to be valid and to show the same route (Appendix D.1 ). sections.heading: Visual spatial planning.
sections.text: VSP [ 15 ] asks for a path through a FrozenLake grid from the start to the goal without stepping into a hole; any such path counts as a success. We adapt the finetuned SigLIP2 model for 5k updates on 55.9k maps of sizes 3 × 3 3{\times}3 to 6 × 6 6{\times}6 , synthesized by us or drawn from ThinkMorph [ 57 ] , with all benchmark maps removed, and evaluate on the official 100 maps per level (Table 8 ). JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at levels 3 to 6, on par with the fine variant of LatentUM (99%), which plans visually step by step, and above its coarse variant (85%), ThinkMorph (76%), and InternVL3.5-38B (20%). On larger map sizes not seen in training, it solves 94% at level 7 and 69% at level 8. Its image and text outputs agree on 99.6% of our own test maps. Appendix D.4 describes the setup and the baselines. On the unseen sizes, the drawn path is right more often than the moves, although the image test is the stricter one. At levels 7 and 8, the drawn path is a shortest route on 99% and 96% of maps, while the moves reach the goal on 94% and 69% (Figure 12 a shows a solved map of each size). Of the 37 failures there, 29 lose one move from the reference route while the drawn path is exactly that route. The rate of lost moves grows with the length of the run of repeated moves, from under 2% of runs of one or two moves to 7 of the 9 runs of six, a length that a shortest route cannot have on the sizes used in adaptation. The outputs mostly settle early: on 574 of the 600 maps, both are fixed from the first of 16 steps. Coupled sampling can still restore a lost move (Figure 12 b). On nine maps the moves fail at the first step and solve the map at the end, seven of them with the drawn path fixed throughout, and no map solved at the first step ends unsolved. On the unseen sizes, as on mazes, the image is the more reliable modality, and these text errors match the cost in exact wording that Section 4.2 finds for continuous text.

sections.heading: 6  Conclusion
sections.text: JUICE models the joint distribution of images and text within frozen pretrained representation spaces, using a single flow matching backbone. Because each modality has its own noise level, image generation, visual understanding, and joint generation become paths through one square of noise levels, all handled by the same model. Our pretraining studies point to four principles. Text can be generated as continuous states at little cost to image generation, which stays close to that of a model trained only for text-to-image generation; what suffers is mainly exact wording. Training needs both the edges of the square, where sampling is conditioned on clean context, and the interior, which joint generation passes through. Semantic encoder spaces are better generation targets than spaces built for reconstruction. And a preference between image spaces found at one scale carries over across 179M to 2.1B parameters for captioning but not for generation. At 2.1B parameters and without language model initialization, the backbone is competitive in compositional image generation, in generation that needs world knowledge, and, on several perception benchmarks, in visual understanding. Since the model learns the joint distribution, it can also draw a route and write the matching moves together. On mazes with multiple solutions, coupled sampling makes the two agree without a fixed generation order, and on visual spatial planning it solves nearly all maps of the training sizes. In such a model, the order in which modalities are generated is no longer fixed by the architecture: it becomes a choice at sampling time, and coupled sampling can leave it open. Pretrained continuous spaces thus let one model understand, generate, and coordinate images and text without putting either one first. Limitations and Future Work. The models run at a native 224 × 224 224{\times}224 resolution, which limits fine visual detail. Exact wording lags behind autoregressive text, and without a language model backbone the models trail most of those initialized from LLMs on benchmarks that need domain knowledge, such as AI2D and MMMU. Each pretraining configuration was run once, and the joint reasoning tasks are synthetic planning problems. The next steps follow from these limits: higher resolution, more accurate continuous text, and joint generation on real tasks in which several pairs of image and text outputs are valid.

sections.text: The transformation N m N_{m} in Section 3.3 defines the spaces in which diffusion noise is added. Its form depends on the encoder (Table 11 ). For the RAE representations, we use LayerNorm per token without affine parameters [ 7 , 2 ] . For each of them, we compute a mean and a standard deviation for every feature channel over valid text positions in the training data, keep these statistics fixed, and use the same transformation in training and at inference. All token positions share the statistics, and no extra scalar divisor is applied. sections.text: The default encoders produce 256 image tokens with 1,152 channels and 128 text tokens with 512 channels. The default 668M MM-RiT has two input layers for text only (which we empirically add) followed by 17 joint attention blocks, with four time tokens per modality.

sections.heading: A.4.1  Image decoders
sections.text: Each image representation uses its corresponding reconstruction decoder. Following the representation autoencoder construction of Zheng et al. [6] , our SigLIP2-SO400M and WebSSL-DINO encoders use their corresponding pretrained Scale-RAE decoders [ 7 ] . The VAE encoder uses its pretrained VAE decoder, and the pixel arm uses an unpatchification head.

sections.heading: A.4.2  Text decoders
sections.text: Each text representation has its own decoder, trained on text alone and kept fixed during MM-RiT training, and all quantitative text results outside the decoder comparison of Table 15 are read out in one pass: captions and answers to questions by parallel decoders, and the moves of the planning tasks by linear task heads. Flan-T5 states have two parallel decoders. The parallel caption decoder is trained on the pretraining captions alone for 3,000 steps; it reads out the captioning results of the pretraining study and gives the Flan-T5 entry of the parallel decoder row in Table 29 . The final parallel decoder, described next, is trained on captions and question answering text and reads out the question answering results of the final models. The other text representations use their own parallel decoders (below). In the mazes and in VSP, the moves are read from the generated text states by a linear head trained for each task (end of this section), not by a parallel decoder. An autoregressive decoder over the same states, described below, serves as a comparison and reads out the qualitative joint samples (Figures 10 , 19 , 20 , and 21 ).

sections.heading: Final parallel decoder.
sections.text: The decoder maps the 128 generated text states to 128 tokens in one forward pass. It is a copy of the Flan-T5-Small encoder stack (8 layers) followed by a vocabulary head. Every position attends to every other position, so the decoder needs no answer length as input; the decoded text is the token sequence before the first predicted EOS. We train the decoder alone, on text only, without MM-RiT: the inputs are the frozen Flan-T5-Small states of the captions and “Question: … Answer: …” rows in the pretraining data, and no images are used. The decoder reads unnormalized encoder states: generated states are multiplied by 0.2 (Appendix A.2 ) before decoding. The loss is cross entropy at all 128 positions; content and EOS positions have weight 1, and padding positions are labeled EOS with weight 0.2. There are two training stages of 8,000 steps each, with 64 texts per step. Stage one starts from the pretrained Flan-T5-Small encoder stack, and stage two picks up where it ended. The optimizer is AdamW with a constant learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} and no weight decay; we clip gradients at 1.0, run bfloat16 autocast over float32 weights, and keep the T5 dropout of 0.1. One stage takes about 1.3 hours on a single A100 GPU.

sections.heading: Comparison with an autoregressive decoder.
sections.text: We compare the parallel decoder with an autoregressive decoder that reads the same states and with a linear readout head (described at the end of this section). The autoregressive decoder is the Flan-T5-Small decoder (8 layers, width 512, 6 heads, feedforward width 1,024, gated GELU) with the frozen Flan-T5-Small vocabulary head (58.1M parameters in total). It attends to the 128 unnormalized states through cross attention and decodes greedily with a KV cache. We train only its blocks and final layer norm (25.2M parameters) with teacher forcing and cross entropy on the content tokens and the final EOS, perturbing half of each batch with the same noise per position as above (AdamW, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , no weight decay, 64 texts per step). For captions, we take a version of this decoder that was already finetuned on perturbed states and train it for 1,500 more steps on caption states; we call the result the autoregressive caption decoder. For question answering, we train it for 3,000 more steps on the VQAv2 training split. Under teacher forcing, the decoder input starts with the “Question: … Answer:” prefix, and the loss covers only the answer and EOS. Answer positions are perturbed, and the positions after the answer are kept, set to zero, or replaced by noise, each with equal probability. On 300 VQAv2 validation questions, this raises its VQA accuracy on clean answer states from 61.2% to 95.9%. On captions held out from training, the parallel decoder recovers almost every token and 98.4% of captions exactly from clean states. It keeps most of this accuracy (93.7%) when the clean fraction of each state drops to 0.7, whereas the autoregressive decoder falls to 58.5% (Table 14 ). The linear head recovers 98.7% of tokens but only 50.8% of captions exactly, and its EOS error of 10.5 positions indicates that it often misplaces the end of the text. On answer states generated by JUICE, the two decoders are within 1.5 points on VQA benchmarks with open answers (VQAv2, OK-VQA, GQA), with the autoregressive decoder slightly ahead on most of them and on MME-P. On most multiple choice benchmarks the parallel decoder is far ahead, for example 66.0 vs. 45.3 on MMBench, while on MMMU the two are within 1.8 points (Table 15 ). The training data of the parallel decoder include multiple choice answers given as option letters, whereas the question answering stage of the autoregressive decoder uses only VQAv2 answers, so the gap on multiple choice benchmarks reflects training data at least in part and cannot be attributed to the decoding scheme alone. The autoregressive decoder needs one forward pass per generated token, so its cost rises with the length of the output. For timing, we use one A100 80GB PCIe GPU (PyTorch 2.5.1, TF32 disabled), do two warmup runs, and synchronize the GPU before and after every timed call. On 2,000 captions of 84.6 tokens on average, with both decoders in bfloat16, the autoregressive decoder is 116, 163, 98, and 54 times slower than the parallel decoder at batch sizes 1, 16, 64, and 128. On VQAv2 answers of 1.6 tokens on average, again with both decoders in bfloat16, it is 3.9 times slower at batch size 1 (30.89 ms against 7.86 ms per answer) and 6.4 times slower at batch size 128, where it groups answers by prefix length (1.630 ms against 0.254 ms per answer). With both decoders in float32, the ratios are 4.1 and 2.1: at batch size 128, bfloat16 makes the parallel decoder 2.8 times faster but the autoregressive decoder slightly slower (1.501 ms per answer in float32). sections.heading: Training times per token.
sections.text: We extend these task choices to partial inputs by varying time across positions, following the noising per token of Diffusion Forcing [ 58 ] . We first complete encoding and normalization (Appendix A.2 ), and then apply span masks and times per token only to the normalized target latents. For each target stream, with probability 15 % 15\% , only a contiguous target span is corrupted and the remaining target positions stay clean. With probability 10 % 10\% , target positions independently draw their times; otherwise they share the stream time. The same interpolation is applied at each selected latent position. These operations do not construct the clean VQA question condition, which uses the independent encoding of the question alone described below.

sections.heading: Parameter updates.
sections.text: For each microbatch, the frozen encoders produce the representations, each example gets a denoising task, and the targets are corrupted at the sampled times. MM-RiT predicts the clean representations, and the loss above updates its parameters, including the input and output projections. Encoders, image decoders, and text decoders do not change in this stage. We also keep two exponential moving averages (EMA) of the MM-RiT weights, with the decay rates given in Table 22 .

sections.heading: B.1.1  Framework implementations
sections.text: Figure 13 summarizes the four generative configurations compared in Table 2 . All use an MM-RiT trunk of width 1,216 with two streams, 17 joint blocks, two input layers for text only, 19 attention heads of dimension 64, and four time tokens per modality, trained under the same schedule of 50k updates. The configurations differ in their state representations, generation objectives, attention masks, and output interfaces.

sections.heading: Text representations and conditioning.
sections.text: In the base framework comparison, only JUICE uses the frozen Flan-T5-Small encoder for both clean conditioning states and continuous generation targets. Appendix B.1.2 additionally supplies frozen T5 states to the clean text condition branch of the discrete text configurations, while retaining their original generated targets and objectives. The other three configurations use discrete text tokens with learned embeddings and token prediction heads. The base token configurations reuse the T5 tokenizer and its vocabulary of 32,128 entries, but do not run the T5 encoder for either clean conditioning text or generated text targets. Their clean text conditions enter the backbone directly through token embeddings. Thus, sharing a tokenizer does not imply sharing pretrained contextual text representations. Figure 13: Four generative configurations at a shared MM-RiT trunk scale. JUICE uses frozen SigLIP2 and T5 features for continuous image and text generation. The token controls use learned text embeddings without a T5 encoder; only the tokenizer and vocabulary are shared. The first three configurations use continuous SigLIP2 image states, whereas the fully discrete control uses VQ image codes. MSE and CE denote mean squared error and cross entropy, respectively.

sections.heading: Continuous image and text (JUICE).
sections.text: At 224 × 224 224{\times}224 , the image stream holds 256 frozen SigLIP2 states with 1,152 channels and the text stream 128 frozen T5 states with 512 channels. Both streams are generated with continuous flow matching, each with its own sampled time. The bidirectional trunk predicts clean states; we turn them into velocities for the stabilized velocity loss on generated image tokens and valid text positions. During Euler sampling, both streams are advanced from the same current pair of image and text. The matched RAE decoder gives the image, and the parallel text decoder (Appendix A.4.2 ) reads all final text states in one pass, cutting the text at the first predicted EOS.

sections.heading: Continuous image and autoregressive text (Transfusion-style).
sections.text: This control keeps the continuous SigLIP2 image stream and predicts text tokens autoregressively instead of generating text states with flow matching. At text target positions, the inputs are the token embeddings shifted by one, with the mask token as the start symbol, and the input embedding matrix is shared with the output head. Valid text positions are trained with cross entropy on the next token. In examples with text targets, text queries attend causally, and image and time queries cannot attend to text target keys, so future tokens cannot leak to earlier text positions through the other streams. A clean text condition for image generation stays fully visible through its token embeddings. Images are generated by Euler integration and decoded with the RAE decoder, and text is decoded greedily up to EOS.

sections.heading: Continuous image and masked text (D-DiT-style).
sections.text: Here the image stream stays continuous (SigLIP2), but text becomes a canvas of discrete tokens [ 18 ] . Each text target token is masked with probability 1 − t t 1-t_{\mathrm{t}} ; the text time therefore controls how many tokens are visible. Visible tokens enter the bidirectional trunk through their embeddings, and masked ones through a learned mask embedding. We train masked valid text positions with cross entropy and keep the continuous velocity loss for the image. For sampling, the text canvas starts fully masked, and a cosine schedule reveals the most confident positions step by step. The image is sampled with Euler updates.

sections.heading: Masked image and text (MMaDA-style).
sections.text: Here both modalities are discrete [ 3 ] . Images become a 16 × 16 16\times 16 canvas of aMUSEd VQ codes (codebook of 8,192 entries, 256 × 256 256\times 256 input). Image and text targets are masked independently according to their modality times and trained with cross entropy on the masked tokens. The embeddings of both canvases go into the bidirectional trunk with two streams, and at sampling time each canvas is unmasked in order of confidence with a cosine schedule. The frozen VQ decoder turns the image codes into pixels, and the text tokens are read up to EOS.

sections.heading: B.1.2  Matching the text-to-image conditioning encoder
sections.text: In their base form, the Transfusion-style, D-DiT-style, and MMaDA-style frameworks condition image generation on token embeddings, while JUICE conditions on contextual frozen T5 states. To see how much this matters, we give each token configuration the same frozen Flan-T5-Small states in its clean T2I condition branch. Nothing else changes: the generated text stays discrete, with the original autoregressive or masked token objective and readout, and the image representation and image objective are the same as before. We use the 668M backbone family, 50k pretraining updates, and the common guidance setting ( w = 5 w=5 with the generic caption reference). Table 2 in the main text includes these rows. Replacing token embeddings with T5 raises Transfusion-style GenEval from 44.23 to 46.07 (a gain of 1.84 points) and DPG from 76.84 to 78.24 (a gain of 1.40 points). This GenEval gain of 1.84 points accounts for part of the original gap of 4.18 points to JUICE; the remaining gap in the point estimate is 2.34 points. D-DiT-style gains 3.08 points in GenEval and 1.96 points in DPG, while MMaDA-style gains 1.74 points in GenEval and 1.96 points in DPG. Their remaining gaps may reflect other differences in the generation configuration, which this comparison does not isolate: D-DiT-style retains a masked token objective for text, and MMaDA-style also uses a VQ image interface with masked image generation.

sections.heading: Dual conditional (DC) control.
sections.text: Each example assigned to the original joint branch gets two conditional forward passes instead of one joint pass: one predicts the image from clean text, and the other predicts the text from the clean image. Both reuse the sampled target masks, corruption times, and noises. We sum the two target loss numerators and divide by the same active target counts of each modality as in Mixing, followed by one optimizer update; averaging the two branches separately and adding them would double the loss scale. The original conditional branches are kept.

sections.heading: Blocked joint control.
sections.text: This control keeps everything about the joint branch (both targets, their noise, the task probabilities, and the loss reduction) except that image and text cannot see each other on joint examples. We mask every path between the two modalities at every layer, including paths through shared time or auxiliary tokens. Shared tokens are duplicated per modality, and each copy carries only its own modality’s information. The conditional branches stay as they are.

sections.heading: Single target joint control.
sections.text: Joint examples keep both streams noisy, but only one modality, picked with probability 1 / 2 1/2 , is supervised, and the other stream serves only as context. sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Mixing ends 2.51 GenEval and 1.08 CIDEr ahead of matched DC after 50k updates, and 2.92 GenEval and 2.22 CIDEr ahead of blocked joint. DC alters the clean or noisy context and the computation at the same time, so this comparison alone cannot tell how much semantic information the noisy partner provides. Still, the results fit a contribution from cross-modal exchange beyond the target count. Compared with Multi-task at 50k updates, DC with matched work (32.1k updates, the same work) gains 6.9 GenEval but loses 7.9 CIDEr and 2.5 DPG. Because this is a mixed result and not a uniform gain, we draw our conclusions about joint training from the matched DC and blocked joint controls.

sections.heading: Dataset construction.
sections.text: We construct a variant of the maze task with multiple solutions [ 14 ] to evaluate the correctness and consistency of jointly generated image and text outputs. Starting from grid mazes generated by randomized depth first search, we remove additional walls at dead ends to introduce cycles. We sample distinct start and goal cells and retain puzzles with between two and sixteen shortest routes. For each training example, we uniformly select one shortest route and use it to construct both targets: an image with the route painted blue and its corresponding sequence of moves from { U , D , L , R } \{\mathrm{U},\mathrm{D},\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}\} . Thus, each training pair is consistent, while a given puzzle admits multiple valid output pairs. The model receives an unsolved maze image together with a text question that gives the grid size and the start and goal coordinates. Images are 224 × 224 224{\times}224 , and each maze block lines up with one 14 × 14 14\times 14 image patch. Walls, background, and the start and goal markers are part of the input, and the model draws the route. There are 200,000 training examples with grids of 5 × 5 5\times 5 , 6 × 6 6\times 6 , and 7 × 7 7\times 7 . We test on 500 puzzles (167, 167, and 166 of the three sizes) whose layouts do not appear in the training set, and at evaluation we accept any valid shortest route, not only the route stored as the target.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We initialize the 2.1B models from the raw weights of the SFT stage (step 15,000; Table 23 ) and adapt them for 5,000 updates. We use AdamW with a global batch size of 1,024, a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 250 warmup steps, and weight decay 0.01 0.01 . The joint adaptation uses 50% joint generation examples, 25% image generation examples conditioned on text, and 25% text generation examples conditioned on images (4, 2, and 2 of every 8 rows in a microbatch, from nominal weights 0.6, 0.2, and 0.2). The Image FT only and Text FT only models are finetuned (FT) on the image or the text target alone; Table 7 reports the validity of that modality.

sections.heading: Inference and evaluation.
sections.text: At inference, the given image patches and question tokens remain fixed, while the image target and answer positions are initialized from noise. Coupled sampling evaluates both velocity fields from the same current state of image and text and advances both generated streams at each Euler step. For sequential sampling, one sampler first generates the solved image and then runs image-to-text generation to get the text solution, while the other generates text first and then runs text-to-image generation. In all samplers, the linear task head of the mazes reads the moves from the generated text states (Appendix A.4.2 ). We use three measures. Image validity (I) checks that the decoded route is a legal shortest path from start to goal, and text validity (T) applies the same check to the move sequence. Joint success (J) further asks that both outputs show the same route. If the image and the moves each give a valid but different shortest route, the sample fails.

Without guidance, coupled sampling gets both velocity fields from the shared state in a single forward pass and then advances both streams. Independent sampling advances each stream on its own, with the other stream left at its initial noise. Sequential sampling completes the first stream, then uses its clean output as the condition for the second. For SigLIP2, image first is therefore better than coupled sampling, while for DINO the two do not differ significantly. sections.heading: D.3  Maze trajectory case studies
sections.text: Figure 11 shows mazes 37 and 61, in which coupled sampling reaches agreement while independent sampling ends with two valid but different routes. In maze 37 (Figure 11 a), the moves are fixed from the first step and the drawn route changes to their route at step 3; in maze 61 (Figure 11 b), the drawn route is fixed from step 2 and the moves change to it at step 7. Both directions also occur in other mazes of the same run: the drawn route changes in maze 208, and the moves change in maze 23. Their independent counterparts again end with two valid but different routes.

sections.heading: D.4  Visual spatial planning
sections.text: VSP [ 15 ] poses navigation problems on FrozenLake grids. The input is an image of the map with the start, the goal, and holes, and the answer is a sequence of moves (U, D, L, R) that reaches the goal without stepping into a hole; any such sequence counts as a success, and moves off the grid leave the player in place. Levels 3 to 8 correspond to 3 × 3 3{\times}3 to 8 × 8 8{\times}8 grids, with 100 test maps per level. As for the mazes, JUICE generates the map with the path drawn on it and the move sequence together, with coupled sampling, 16 steps, and no guidance, and a linear task head reads the moves (Appendix A.4.2 ). We adapt the finetuned SigLIP2 model for 5,000 updates (Table 23 ) on maps of sizes 3 × 3 3{\times}3 to 6 × 6 6{\times}6 , so levels 7 and 8 use map sizes that do not appear in training. The training set has 55,939 maps. We generate FrozenLake maps with random start and goal positions and a hole probability drawn from 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.35 ) \mathcal{U}(0,0.35) , keep only solvable maps, and use the shortest path found by breadth first search as the target route, breaking ties in the order L, U, D, R. After removing duplicates and every map that appears in the VSP benchmark, 50,000 generated maps remain. The other 5,939 maps are the 6,000 FrozenLake problems of ThinkMorph [ 57 ] without the 61 that coincide with benchmark maps. All maps are rendered again on a 224 × 224 224{\times}224 canvas in which each cell covers 2 × 2 2\times 2 SigLIP2 patches, and the target image draws the route in red. Adaptation uses the optimizer settings and task ratios of the maze recipe (Appendix D.1 ). We score the move sequences with the official evaluation script on the 100 benchmark maps of each level. The main metric averages levels 3 to 6, the sizes seen in training, and levels 7 and 8 measure extrapolation to larger maps. The official rule checks only the move sequence; on 500 maps of our own held out from training, we also check that the drawn path and the moves agree (joint consistency, 99.6%). On the benchmark maps of levels 3 to 8, the drawn path is a shortest route on 98, 100, 100, 99, 99, and 96 of the 100 maps, and the moves reach the goal on 100, 100, 100, 99, 94, and 69. We split each reference route into runs of the same repeated move. On levels 7 and 8, the generated moves drop exactly one move from 2 of the 238 runs of length one, from 2 of 117 runs of length two, 4 of 81 of length three, 7 of 45 of length four, 7 of 23 of length five, and 7 of 9 of length six. On levels 3 to 6, no move is dropped from any of the 810 runs. The baseline values in Table 8 are taken from LatentUM [ 55 ] . InternVL3.5-38B [ 56 ] is evaluated without training for the task, using the official VSP prompt. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.28801v1 [cs.CV] 20 Oct 2026 JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces Jiahan Li 1,* , Huangyuan Su 2 , Shengbang Tong 1 , Shusheng Yang 1 , Ruihan Guo 3 Suozhi Huang 4 , Hexu Zhao 1 , Pratyusha Sharma 1 , Sherry Yang 1 , Jiatao Gu 5 Rob Fergus 1,† , Kyunghyun Cho 1,† 1 New York University 2 Harvard University 3 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 4 Princeton University 5 University of Pennsylvania * Project lead: jl17319@nyu.edu † Equal advising Code https://github.com/Ced3-han/JUICE-Code Weights https://huggingface.co/collections/CedLJH/juice Blog https://ced3-han.github.io/JUICE-Website/ Abstract Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224 × 224 224{\times}224 , JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes. Key Takeaways T1. Unified model : one flow matching model generates both images and text; with its own noise level for each modality, the same weights handle every task. § 3 T2. Pretrained encoder spaces : both modalities are generated as continuous states of frozen encoders; at equal guidance, image quality holds and captions lose only exact wording. § 4.2 T3. Joint training : adding joint denoising, with both modalities noisy, to the conditional tasks improves image generation and captioning alike. § 4.3 T4. Encoder choice : semantic encoders beat VAE latents and pixels; SigLIP2, aligned with language, helps captioning most, and Flan-T5 gives the best text space. § 4.4 T5. Scaling behavior : every metric improves with model size, but rankings can flip: DINO leads image generation at 179M and SigLIP2 at 2.1B. § 4.5 T6. Joint reasoning : sampled together, image and text adjust to each other, so a drawn route and its written moves agree without a fixed order. § 5.4 1 Introduction Unified multimodal models aim to understand and generate both images and text within a single model. Most current systems, however, treat the two modalities asymmetrically. In the dominant design, a pretrained autoregressive language model generates text and drives a diffusion or flow matching head that generates images [ 1 , 2 ] ; other models quantize images and generate both modalities as discrete tokens [ 3 , 4 ] . Either way, the two modalities are generated by different processes or through a quantizer, and the joint distribution is factorized in a fixed order: an output that contains both an image and text is produced one modality after the other, and the first cannot be revised in light of the second. Vision is also usually added to a model that was first pretrained on language, although controlled studies of multimodal pretraining find that late integration makes models lean on language priors and that training the modalities jointly from the start works better [ 5 ] . This suggests a different design: a model that treats both modalities alike, generates them with one process, and learns them together from the start. Such a design needs two things: a space in which one process can generate both modalities, and a source of knowledge for a backbone trained without a language model. Frozen pretrained encoders provide both. Their spaces are continuous for images and text alike and carry visual and linguistic knowledge learned at scale, and recent studies show that they are good generative targets for vision [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and for language [ 9 ] , although they were never built for generation. In these spaces, one flow matching process generates both modalities with the same objective, the same features serve as targets and as context, and a model of the joint distribution also contains its conditionals. Give each modality its own noise level and the two levels span a square (Figure 2 ). Text-to-image generation, captioning, and question answering hold one modality clean and move along an edge. Joint generation cuts through the middle, where image and text take shape together. To build a working model on this idea, we had to settle four questions that existing unified models leave open: whether text should be generated as continuous states or kept as tokens, which denoising tasks to train on, which encoder spaces to read and write, and whether these answers still hold as the model grows. We introduce JUICE ( J oint U nified multimodal modeling I n C ontinuous E ncoder spaces; Figure 1 ), a unified model that works directly in the continuous spaces of frozen pretrained image and text encoders. A single flow matching backbone, MM-RiT, trained from scratch, connects the image and text streams through bidirectional joint attention [ 10 ] , and each stream has its own noise scale and schedule. We train MM-RiT on both the edges and the interior of the square, with conditional and joint denoising. At inference, a task is a path through the square: keeping some streams clean ( t = 1 t=1 ) and generating the others gives text-to-image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or coupled joint generation (Section 3 ). Figure 1: JUICE overview. (a) Continuous image and text representations from frozen encoders share one MM-RiT backbone via bidirectional joint attention. Appendix A.3 explains the details of each block. (b) Conditional tasks (text-to-image, visual question answering) and joint reasoning (maze solving) use the same interface by assigning clean context ( t = 1 t{=}1 ) and generation targets ( t < 1 t{<}1 ). Our pretraining studies (Section 4 ) change one design choice at a time and keep the rest of the recipe fixed. (i) Generative frameworks. At a shared guidance scale, JUICE scores 48.41 GenEval and a model trained only for text-to-image generation scores 47.86, while all three frameworks that write text as tokens fall below that model. Captions generated as continuous states lose some exact wording but match the images as well as autoregressive captions do. (ii) Training task mixtures. Training should cover the regions that sampling visits: joint and conditional denoising together outperform either one alone, beyond the effect of supervising more targets. (iii) Representation spaces. The VAE reconstructs better than the semantic encoders, yet generation and captioning both work better in the semantic spaces, and Flan-T5 states beat larger text embedding models. (iv) Scaling. From 179M to 2.1B backbone parameters, SigLIP2 [ 11 ] , which is aligned with language, writes better captions at every size, while the early lead of WebSSL-DINO [ 12 ] (DINO) in image generation disappears. With these answers in hand, we train two 2.1B models that pair Flan-T5 with SigLIP2 or with DINO (Section 5 ). Working at 224 × 224 224{\times}224 and starting from no language model, each uses one set of weights for compositional image generation, generation that needs world knowledge, and visual question answering. The two reach 0.87 and 0.88 GenEval, and the SigLIP2 model reaches 85.22 on DPG-Bench, 0.45 on WISE [ 13 ] , and 73.1 on VQAv2. Because JUICE models the joint distribution, it can also reason jointly across modalities: with coupled sampling, the image and its text are generated together, each conditioning on the other’s evolving state. We adapt JUICE to two planning tasks, mazes with multiple solutions [ 14 ] and visual spatial planning [ 15 ] , in which it draws a route on the map and writes the matching moves. Sampled independently, the two outputs often disagree on mazes: the model draws one valid route and writes out a different one, and joint success is only 54.6%. Generating one modality first repairs this, but the result then depends on the order (95.2% with the image first, 85.3% with the text first), and nothing says in advance which order to use. Coupled sampling reaches 93.7% without making that choice. In the two cases we trace, whichever output settles later rewrites itself to match the other. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at the training sizes, and 94% and 69% at two larger sizes it never saw in training. Our main contributions are: 1. Joint modeling in pretrained representation spaces. We propose JUICE, which models the joint distribution of images and text in the continuous spaces of frozen pretrained encoders with one flow matching Transformer trained from scratch. With a noise level for each modality, every task is a path through one square, with no fixed generation order. 2. Systematic design studies. Section 4 reports controlled pretraining runs on how text is generated, which tasks are trained, and which encoder spaces are used, plus a scaling study from 179M to 2.1B parameters. We summarize what they show as four takeaways for continuous joint modeling. 3. Scaling and joint reasoning. A single set of 2.1B weights handles compositional image generation, generation that needs world knowledge, and visual question answering (Section 5 ). On two planning tasks, coupled sampling gets the drawn route and the written moves to agree without a fixed generation order (Section 5.4 ). 2 Related Work Table 1: Generation spaces and processes in multimodal models. AR: autoregressive; FM: flow matching; repr.: representations.
