FM Scale-RAE [ 7 ] Discrete tokens AR Pretrained repr. FM JUICE Pretrained repr. FM Pretrained repr. FM Unified multimodal models. Most unified models are hybrids that combine different representation spaces and generative processes (Table 1 ). Chameleon [ 16 ] models discrete text tokens and quantized image codes autoregressively. Transfusion [ 17 ] pairs autoregressive text with diffusion over continuous image latents, and Show-o [ 20 ] pairs autoregressive text with diffusion over discrete image tokens. MMaDA [ 3 ] and Muddit [ 4 ] use discrete masked diffusion for both modalities, while D-DiT [ 18 ] combines discrete masked diffusion for text with continuous flow for images. D-DiT and Muddit start from pretrained image generators, Show-o and MMaDA from pretrained language models, and Chameleon and Transfusion are trained from scratch. In most of these models, the two modalities are generated by different processes, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order. JUICE instead generates both with one flow matching process in frozen representation spaces and is trained from scratch; Section 4.2 compares it with representative formulations under the same recipe. Generation in pretrained representation spaces. Representation autoencoders (RAEs) [ 6 , 7 ] show that diffusion works well on frozen pretrained visual features, whose semantic structure makes them good targets. Beyond Language Modeling (BLM) [ 8 ] takes up this idea and trains a unified backbone from scratch with flow matching over frozen visual features, while language is still predicted autoregressively as discrete tokens. Other unified models pick different visual targets. Show-o2 [ 1 ] still generates VAE latents, which it processes semantically. TUNA [ 21 ] aligns unified features built from VAE latents, and Tuna-2 [ 2 ] removes the visual encoders altogether and generates pixels. For text, ELF [ 9 ] applies continuous flow matching directly in pretrained text representation spaces, though only to generate text on its own. Each of these works generates only one modality in a continuous representation space: BLM still predicts text as tokens, and ELF generates no images. JUICE generates both modalities in pretrained spaces with one process, so the same representations serve as generation targets and as cross-modal context, and Sections 4.4 and 4.5 study which spaces suit this joint use and how the answer changes with scale. Joint and conditional multimodal modeling. Separate noise schedules for each modality [ 19 , 22 ] provide a mathematical framework for a single model to capture the marginal, conditional, and joint distributions of images and text. Existing implementations, however, need specialized components. UniDiffuser [ 19 ] diffuses CLIP embeddings and needs a separate autoregressive GPT-2 to decode text; OneFlow [ 23 ] models text with discrete edit flows. OmniFlow [ 24 ] uses rectified flow for generation from any modality to any other. Its MMDiT backbone starts from Stable Diffusion 3, and its text latent comes from a VAE built on Flan-T5 and TinyLlama. JUICE keeps both modalities as continuous encoder states with one state per token, decodes text with a lightweight parallel decoder, and trains one backbone on them from scratch. In this setting, joint denoising improves conditional generation by more than its extra targets explain (Section 4.3 ), and coupled sampling lets the two streams settle on the same one of several valid solutions (Section 5.4 ). Continuous diffusion for language. Early work diffused learned word embeddings and rounded them back to tokens (Diffusion-LM [ 25 ] , DiffuSeq [ 26 ] ); later work improved the likelihood objectives (CDCD [ 27 ] , Plaid [ 28 ] ). Flow matching over categorical distributions, which places each token on the probability simplex, offers another continuous route to discrete data such as text [ 29 , 30 ] . A second line of work diffuses directly in the representation spaces of pretrained language models, either after compressing sequences into fixed latents (LD4LG [ 31 ] ) or over contextual encoder states (TEncDM [ 32 ] , ELF [ 9 ] ). JUICE follows the second line for its text stream and diffuses contextual encoder states. Unlike these text only models, it generates the states jointly with images, and Section 4.2 compares this choice with discrete text under one recipe. 3 Method As shown in Figure 1 , JUICE operates directly in the continuous representation spaces of frozen pretrained encoders, using a single flow matching Transformer (MM-RiT) trained from scratch. The same model supports generation, understanding, and joint tasks over images and text simply by varying which representations are provided as clean inputs and which are generated from noise. Section 3.1 reviews flow matching, Section 3.2 presents the formulation, and Sections 3.3 to 3.5 describe the architecture, training procedure, and inference; Appendix A.6 provides implementation details. 3.1 Preliminaries Flow matching [ 33 ] trains a network to predict a velocity field that, over time, transports a noise distribution to the data distribution. Setting t m = 1 t_{m}{=}1 makes modality m m a clean condition, and any t m < 1 t_{m}{<}1 means it is still being generated. A task is thus just a path through the square. Text-to-image generation follows the edge t t = 1 t_{\mathrm{t}}{=}1 and captioning the edge t i = 1 t_{\mathrm{i}}{=}1 , while joint generation cuts through the interior. Question answering sets times per token, so the image and the question stay at t = 1 t{=}1 while the answer is generated (Appendix A.6.2 ). We therefore train on the edges with conditional denoising and on the interior with joint denoising, so that every region sampling passes through is covered. The formulation introduces three requirements, each addressed by one design component. First, because the two representation spaces differ in dimensionality and feature statistics, each modality has its own projections, noise scale, and noise schedule (Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). Second, because any token can be either a condition or a generation target, time tokens in the sequence and a time embedding for each token tell the network the role of each position (Section 3.3 ). Each modality has its own time, from noise ( t = 0 t{=}0 ) to clean ( t = 1 t{=}1 ). Conditional tasks run along the edges, where the condition is clean, and joint generation crosses the interior; its path bends because the image schedule keeps the image noisier for longer. Training covers both regions: conditional denoising on the edges and joint denoising in the interior. 3.3 Architecture Representation Encoders. Given a paired image x i x_{\mathrm{i}} and text x t x_{\mathrm{t}} , frozen pretrained encoders extract features that are normalized to align their scales with the diffusion noise [ 35 ] : h m = E m ​ ( x m ) , z m = N m ​ ( h m ) , m ∈ { i , t } . h_{m}=E_{m}(x_{m}),\qquad z_{m}=N_{m}(h_{m}),\qquad m\in\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{t}\}. (3) SigLIP2 [ 11 ] and Flan-T5-Small [ 36 ] are our default image and text encoders, and Section 4.4 looks at other choices. We do not finetune the encoders. Their spaces already encode visual and linguistic knowledge learned at scale, and if they stay fixed, the same features can be used both as targets to generate and as context to condition on. Multimodal Representation Diffusion Transformer (MM-RiT). MM-RiT implements f θ f_{\theta} in Equation 2 : it receives both streams at independently specified noise levels ( t i , t t ) (t_{\mathrm{i}},t_{\mathrm{t}}) [ 19 ] and predicts both denoised clean states, which we convert to velocities for training (velocity matching loss) and inference (ODE solver). To accommodate the distinct image and text representation spaces, each MM-RiT block uses separate Q/K/V projections for each modality, concatenates the resulting sequences for one bidirectional joint attention operation, and then applies separate output projections and feedforward networks [ 7 , 8 , 37 ] . Time tokens in the sequence and additive time embeddings for each token expose the noise level of each modality and each token, so the network can distinguish clean conditioning positions ( t = 1 t{=}1 ) from generation targets ( t < 1 t{<}1 ). Representation Decoders. Fixed decoders map the generated representations back to pixels and tokens at inference: x ^ i = D i ​ ( z i ) , x ^ t = D t ​ ( z t ) . \widehat{x}_{\mathrm{i}}=D_{\mathrm{i}}(z_{\mathrm{i}}),\qquad\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{t}}=D_{\mathrm{t}}(z_{\mathrm{t}}). (4) For images we use the Scale-RAE decoder that belongs to the image encoder [ 7 ] . For text, a lightweight parallel decoder maps all generated states to tokens in one forward pass, which is much faster than autoregressive decoding; the pretraining study and the final models each use one decoder of this design. All decoders are trained separately and stay fixed during MM-RiT training. Appendix A.4 describes them and compares parallel with autoregressive decoding. 3.4 Training Noise and Schedules for Each Modality. Image and text representations differ in dimensionality, scale, and geometry, and noise settings that work for one may not work for the other, so each modality gets its own. First, the Gaussian noise scale is set separately ( σ i = 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}{=}1 , σ t = 2 \sigma_{\mathrm{t}}{=}2 by default) and matched to the statistics of each space after normalization. Second, the noise levels follow a separate distribution for each modality: for modality m m , we draw a base time u m u_{m} from a logit normal distribution and transform it by t m = S α m ​ ( u m ) , S α ​ ( u ) = u α + ( 1 − α ) ​ u . t_{m}=S_{\alpha_{m}}(u_{m}),\qquad S_{\alpha}(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha+(1-\alpha)\,u}. This moves probability mass toward noisier states. Text is not shifted ( α t = 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{t}}{=}1 ). Features of high dimension can keep much of their information at moderate noise levels, so the shift makes the model see states dominated by noise more often [ 10 , 6 ] . (6) Classifier-Free Guidance. For conditional tasks we apply classifier-free guidance [ 38 ] in velocity space: the prediction with the condition is pushed away from a reference prediction without it, which strengthens what the condition adds. No training stage drops the condition, so JUICE has no learned null token. The reference instead replaces the condition with an uninformative input that the model has learned to handle. For an image condition, the image is placed at its noise end, a state the joint task trains the model to see next to text; for a text condition, we use the clean states of the generic caption “a photo.”, which says almost nothing about the image. We use w = 5 w{=}5 for text-to-image generation, w = 3 w{=}3 for captioning and question answering, and no guidance for joint generation and planning. In joint generation, both velocity fields are computed from the current joint state ( z i t i , z t t t ) (z_{\mathrm{i}}^{t_{\mathrm{i}}},z_{\mathrm{t}}^{t_{\mathrm{t}}}) before either modality is updated. We call this coupled sampling . Each stream is thus conditioned, step by step, on the other stream as it evolves. Independent sampling works differently. It integrates each stream separately and leaves the other one at its initial noise for the whole trajectory, which amounts to sampling each modality from its marginal. Sequential sampling first generates one modality completely and then the other conditioned on it, with either the image or the text going first. 4 Pretraining Study Putting both modalities in continuous encoder spaces under one denoiser raises the four questions of Section 1 , and this section takes them in turn. Should text be generated as continuous states or as tokens (Section 4.2 )? Which denoising tasks should training cover (Section 4.3 )? Which encoder spaces should the model read and write (Section 4.4 )? And do the answers change with model size (Section 4.5 )? All runs share the setup below, and each study ends with a takeaway. 4.1 Setup All studies share one pretraining recipe and vary one design choice at a time. The reference model has an MM-RiT backbone with 668M trainable parameters over frozen SigLIP2-SO400M image features and Flan-T5-Small text states. On the alignment between captions and images, JUICE matches autoregressive text (80.20 vs. 80.37 CLIPScore). On n-gram agreement with the reference captions, it is the weakest of the four: its CIDEr (88.80) is just over half that of autoregressive text (160.52) and below D-DiT-style masked text diffusion (115.22). The gap lies mainly in the generated states, not in the parallel caption decoder of this study, which recovers 99.2% of tokens from clean T5 states (Table 29 ; Appendix A.4.2 ). The captions thus describe the image content as well as autoregressive ones but word it differently from the references. This is the pattern expected when errors in a generated continuous state move it toward nearby states with a similar meaning: the wording changes more than the content. Takeaway: Continuous text spares images but costs wording. Of the four frameworks, only the one with continuous text keeps up with a model trained only for text-to-image generation on GenEval at the shared guidance scale (48.41 vs. 47.86); the three token text frameworks all fall below it, even with the T5 condition.
